newsitem.title: DUBAI: UK nurses in Saudi say murder confessions forced.
newsitem.headline: UK nurses in Saudi say murder confessions forced.

text.p: Two British nurses charged with killing an Australian colleague in Saudi Arabia insisted at an Islamic court on Tuesday they were forced into confessing, a legal source close to the case said.

Deborah Parry, 41, and Lucille McLauchlan, 31, clad in traditional long black Moslem robes, appeared calm before a panel of three judges at a second hearing at an Islamic sharia court in the eastern Saudi city of Khobar, the source said.

"Discussion regarding all issues relating to the confessions (by the two nurses) was completed in Tuesday's session and their lawyers presented legal points regarding them," he told Reuters by telephone from Saudi Arabia.
"Both women insisted during the two-hour session that they were forced to make their confessions," the source added.
Saudi authorities were not immediately available for comment.
The two nurses arrived at the court in a police van with tinted glass windows escorted by Saudi policewomen. Witnesses said the nurses, their feet shackled, walked slowly to the courthouse.
Saudi police had said the nurses confessed to the murder of Yvonne Gilford, 55, and the confessions had been filed with three judges.

The law firm of Salah al-Hejailan, which is representing the two nurses, said their clients had withdrawn confessions, and one of them retracted a statement she had had a lesbian relationship with the victim.

Both nurses were charged with murdering Gilford in her dormitory room at the King Fahd medical complex in the eastern oil city of Dhahran on December 11. She had been stabbed, bludgeoned with a hammer and suffocated.
The two women have been imprisoned in the nearby city of Dammam since then.
If convicted of murder, they could face public beheading by the sword, the first time Western women would be executed in the conservative Islamic kingdom.

The attorney representing the family of Gilford on Monday demanded the death penalty for the two nurses, Hejailan's firm said in a statement after the first court hearing on Monday. Gilford's family in Australia had said the two should face the maximum punishment.
Both nurses denied being involved in the murder. Their lawyers said the written confessions were made without legal counsel or access to British diplomats.

"The court began to hear evidence as to the circumstances in which the two British nurses made written statements while in police custody and which they have subsequently withdrawn", the statement said.
"Our clients have withdrawn the written statements given in the days following their arrests without the benefit of counsel and without access to British diplomatic staff," said the statement.
